Textual Defense & Historical Record

The 1611 Authorized Version

The complete scholarly, historical, and documentary case for the King James Bible of 1611 — its translation method, its 47 scholars, its textual lineage, the documented agendas to replace it, the king who authorized it, the assassination attempt made against him for doing so, and the 400-year campaign to discredit the most reliable English Bible ever produced.

⚑ The Core Finding: In 1969, a senior medical figure with direct ties to Planned Parenthood delivered a private address documenting plans to restructure Western civilization — including the specific replacement of the King James Bible through the promotion of competing translations. The proliferation of post-1970 Bible versions maps precisely onto the agenda he described.

I. The New Order of the Barbarians — Primary Source Documentation

The 1969 Address — Source, Provenance, and Context
Dr. Richard Day, M.D., Address to Pittsburgh Pediatric Society, March 20, 1969 · Transcribed by Dr. Lawrence Dunegan, M.D. · Published as The New Order of the Barbarians (also The New World Order) · Pages 36–37 (Religion and Scripture)
On the evening of March 20, 1969, a closed meeting of the Pittsburgh Pediatric Society was addressed by Dr. Richard Day — at that time Professor of Pediatrics at Mount Sinai Medical School in New York City and a former National Medical Director of Planned Parenthood Federation of America. Dr. Lawrence Dunegan, M.D., attended as a physician-member. Day began his remarks with an explicit prohibition: he requested that no notes be taken, no recordings made, and that the content of his address not be attributed to him by name. Dr. Dunegan, recognizing the historical gravity of what he heard, mentally committed the address to memory as carefully as possible. Nearly two decades later, in 1988, Dunegan recorded his recollections across three audio sessions; these recordings were transcribed and published as The New Order of the Barbarians (also published as The New World Order). The document is available in transcript form and has been subject to independent review by researchers who note its specificity: many of the conditions Day described as planned in 1969 have been implemented in the intervening decades with a precision that cannot be dismissed as coincidence. The prohibition on attribution and note-taking — Day's first instruction — is itself evidence that the content was not intended for public knowledge and that he was speaking with the authority of prior knowledge of institutional plans.

Dr. Day identified himself as speaking from within an elite network that had already determined the shape of the society to come. He framed his remarks not as speculation but as disclosure: "I'm going to give you a glimpse of the future," Dunegan recalls him saying, followed by the instruction that what he was about to share was not to leave the room attributed to him. The meeting took place at a private professional gathering — not a public conference — which both explains the candor of the remarks and the limited documentation of the event itself.
Pages 36–37 — The Scripture Replacement Plan
Religion, Bible Versions, and the Controlled Dissolution of Biblical Authority
The section of Dunegan's transcript corresponding to pages 36–37 of the published document addresses the planned treatment of religion and Scripture in the restructured social order. Day's reported remarks on this subject include several interconnected components: (1) Traditional Christianity Would Be Replaced: Day stated that conventional Christian belief — specifically the kind rooted in fixed authoritative Scripture — would be incompatible with the new order. People would not be "using the Bible as it has been in the past." The cultural authority of a single, fixed, word-for-word text would be deliberately undermined. (2) Multiple Competing Translations as the Mechanism: The specific mechanism of replacement was not direct suppression but proliferation — multiple new translations would be produced and promoted, each differing from the others in key passages. The result would be the cultural normalization of the idea that "the Bible says many different things depending on which version you read" — effectively destroying the concept of a single authoritative textual standard. The King James Bible's position as the unquestioned English Scripture would be ended not by banning it but by surrounding it with so many competing alternatives that its authority became merely one option among many. (3) A New "Spirituality" to Replace Scripture-Grounded Faith: Day spoke of a restructured religiosity that would replace doctrinal Christianity — emotional, experiential, non-textual in the traditional sense — that would be socially promoted as the acceptable form of religious expression while text-based, doctrinally precise Christianity was marginalized. Emotional religious experiences without fixed doctrinal content would be encouraged; rigorous Scripture-based theology would be discouraged and eventually viewed as extremist. (4) The Timeline: Day's 1969 projection mapped onto a post-1970 translation timeline with documented precision. The Revised Standard Version had appeared in 1952. The New American Standard Bible arrived in 1971. The New International Version in 1978. The New Revised Standard Version in 1989. The New Living Translation in 1996. The English Standard Version in 2001. The Christian Standard Bible (formerly HCSB) in 2017. Each of these translations departs from the King James Bible in thousands of places, with the cumulative effect Day described: the dissolution of a single textual standard and its replacement by a marketplace of competing "authorized" texts — each produced by committees of scholars from specific theological backgrounds, each encoding those backgrounds into the text itself while presenting the result as objective translation.
The Proliferation Timeline — 1952 to Present
Pre-1952: For 341 years (1611–1952), the King James Bible was the single authoritative English Scripture for Protestant Christianity. No major competing translation had achieved widespread acceptance.

1952 — RSV (Revised Standard Version): American Standard revision, funded by the National Council of Churches. Immediately controversial for its translation of Isaiah 7:14 — rendering "virgin" as "young woman," removing the Messianic virgin birth prophecy from the Old Testament text.

1971 — NASB (New American Standard Bible): Based on the Westcott-Hort Critical Text; strict dynamic equivalence in places; omits or footnotes dozens of KJV verses.

1978 — NIV (New International Version): Most commercially successful modern translation; produced by the International Bible Society; departs from KJV in over 64,000 places (documented by Riplinger, New Age Bible Versions, 1993, p. 56); omits entire verses present in the Byzantine manuscript tradition.

1982 — NKJV (New King James Version): Uses the Received Text but adopts dynamic equivalence translation philosophy in places; includes footnotes promoting Critical Text readings that undermine its own source text.

1989 — NRSV (New Revised Standard Version): Introduces gender-neutral language into Scripture, rendering generic masculine pronouns as gender-neutral — a translation choice driven by 20th-century ideological commitments, not textual evidence.

1996/2004 — NLT (New Living Translation): Fully dynamic equivalence; essentially a paraphrase of the RSV with updated language. Not a translation of the original languages in the formal equivalence sense.

2001 — ESV (English Standard Version): Positioned as a "literal" alternative but based on the Critical Text (Nestle-Aland 27th edition) and departing from KJV in thousands of places.

The Cultural Result: Exactly as Day described — no single authoritative English Bible. A marketplace. Different churches using different versions, often within the same denomination. The concept of "what the Bible says" now contested at the translation level, before any interpretation has begun. A person can cite "the Bible" in support of diametrically opposed positions by selecting different translations — a situation with no parallel in the first 341 years of English Protestant Christianity.

⚑ The Scope: The 1611 KJV was produced by 47 active scholars (from an originally appointed 54) organized into six companies, working simultaneously at Westminster, Oxford, and Cambridge over seven years (1604–1611). No translation in any language has ever been produced by a body of scholars of comparable combined linguistic depth.

I. The Hampton Court Conference — Origin of the Translation

The translation was formally proposed at the Hampton Court Conference of January 14–18, 1604 — a conference convened by King James I to address Puritan ecclesiastical grievances set out in the "Millenary Petition" (signed by approximately 1,000 clergy). On January 16, Dr. John Reynolds (also spelled John Rainolds), President of Corpus Christi College, Oxford, proposed "that there might be a new translation of the Bible, because those which were allowed in the reign of King Henry VIII and Edward VI were corrupt and not answerable to the truth of the Original" (William Barlow, The Summe and Substance of the Conference at Hampton Court, 1604, p. 46). King James responded enthusiastically: "I profess I could never yet see a Bible well translated in English; but I think that, of all, that of Geneva is the worst" (ibid., p. 47) — his objection to the Geneva Bible being its politically charged Calvinist marginal notes, not its scholarship. James then authorized and organized the entire translation enterprise, appointing directors and establishing the rules. He took no further role in the translation decisions themselves.

II. The Six Companies — Members and Responsibilities

Westminster Company #1
Genesis — 2 Kings · Director: Lancelot Andrewes
Lancelot Andrewes — Dean of Westminster, later Bishop of Winchester. Master of 15 languages (Hebrew, Chaldee, Syriac, Greek, Latin, and 10 modern European languages). T.S. Eliot called him "one of the most remarkable men of his generation." Spent 5 hours daily in private devotion and spent the remaining waking hours in scholarship. John Overall — Dean of St. Paul's, later Bishop of Norwich; theologian and linguist. Hadrian à Saravia — Dutch-born theologian; one of the first to argue for foreign missions; polyglot. Richard Clarke — Fellow of Christ's College, Cambridge. John Layfield — Fellow of Trinity College, Cambridge; a noted Greek and Arabic scholar who had traveled to the West Indies and could draw on personal geographical knowledge for relevant passages. Robert Tighe — Archdeacon of Middlesex; Hebrew and Chaldee scholar. Francis Burleigh — Hebrew and Greek scholar. Geoffrey King — Regius Professor of Hebrew, Cambridge. Richard Thomson — Fellow of Clare Hall, Cambridge; known as "Dutch" Thomson for his Netherlands scholarship; polyglot in Hebrew, Greek, Latin, Arabic, and several modern languages. William Bedwell — the foremost English Arabist of his generation; rector of St. Ethelburga's, London; compiled a Persian dictionary and an Arabic lexicon.
Cambridge Company #1
1 Chronicles — Ecclesiastes · Director: Edward Lively (d. 1605) then John Richardson
Edward Lively — Regius Professor of Hebrew at Cambridge; died May 1605, shortly after work began; considered one of the greatest Hebrew scholars in England. John Richardson — Master of Trinity College, Cambridge; took over as director after Lively's death. Lawrence Chaderton — Master of Emmanuel College, Cambridge; Puritan scholar; reportedly preached a sermon of two hours' duration and stopped only when the congregation begged him to continue; lived to 103 years of age. Francis Dillingham — Fellow of Christ's College, Cambridge; Greek and Hebrew scholar. Thomas Harrison — Vice-Master of Trinity College, Cambridge; known for extraordinary memory and depth of learning. Roger Andrewes — brother of Lancelot Andrewes; Master of Jesus College, Cambridge. Robert Spaulding — Fellow of St. John's College, Cambridge. Andrew Bing — Fellow of Peterhouse, Cambridge.
Oxford Company #1
Isaiah — Malachi · Director: John Harding
John Harding — President of Magdalen College, Oxford; Regius Professor of Hebrew. John Reynolds (Rainolds) — President of Corpus Christi College, Oxford; the man who proposed the translation at Hampton Court; Puritan scholar of extraordinary learning; died June 1607 before the work was complete. Thomas Holland — Rector of Exeter College, Oxford; Hebrew and Greek scholar; called by contemporaries "the Atlas of the University." Richard Kilby — Rector of Lincoln College, Oxford; Hebrew scholar. Miles Smith — later Bishop of Gloucester; one of the most learned Hebraists in England; wrote the celebrated preface The Translators to the Reader — itself one of the great prose documents of the age; reportedly able to read Hebrew as easily as English. Richard Brett — Fellow of Lincoln College, Oxford; scholar in Latin, Greek, Hebrew, Aramaic, Arabic, and Ethiopic. Daniel Fairclough — added to the company during the work.
Westminster Company #2
Romans — Jude · Director: William Barlow
William Barlow — Dean of Chester; wrote the account of the Hampton Court Conference. John Spenser — President of Corpus Christi College, Oxford; Greek scholar. Roger Fenton — Fellow of Pembroke College, Cambridge; preacher at Gray's Inn. Ralph Hutchinson — President of St. John's College, Oxford; died 1606 during the translation period. William Dakins — Professor of Divinity, Gresham College; Greek and Hebrew scholar. Michael Rabbett — Fellow of Trinity College, Cambridge. Thomas Sanderson — rector and scholar.
Oxford Company #2
Gospels, Acts, Revelation · Director: Thomas Ravis
Thomas Ravis — Dean of Christ Church, Oxford; later Bishop of London. George Abbot — Dean of Winchester; later Archbishop of Canterbury (1611–1633); his tenure as Archbishop spanned the entire period of the KJV's early distribution. Richard Eedes — Dean of Worcester; royal chaplain. Giles Thomson — Dean of Windsor. Sir Henry Savile — Warden of Merton College, Oxford; the most distinguished classicist of the age; edited the complete works of St. John Chrysostom in 8 folio volumes (Eton, 1610–1613) — a monument of 17th-century scholarship published simultaneously with the KJV. John Peryn — Fellow of New College, Oxford; Greek scholar. Ralph Ravens — Fellow of St. John's College, Oxford. John Harmar — Warden of Winchester College; Greek scholar; produced a translation of Calvin's sermons.
Cambridge Company #2
Apocrypha · Director: John Duport
John Duport — Master of Jesus College, Cambridge; Greek scholar. William Branthwaite — Fellow of Emmanuel College, Cambridge; Greek scholar. Jeremiah Radcliffe — Fellow of Trinity College, Cambridge. Samuel Ward — Fellow of Emmanuel College; later Master of Sidney Sussex College; kept a spiritual diary; attended the Synod of Dort (1618–1619) as one of England's delegates. Andrew Downes — Regius Professor of Greek at Cambridge; so learned that he reportedly could not write a Latin sentence without improving it indefinitely; one of the finest Greek scholars of the era. John Bois — Fellow of St. John's College, Cambridge; the only translator who kept detailed notes of the final revision process — notes discovered at Corpus Christi College, Oxford, and published by Ward Allen as Translating for King James (1969); Bois reportedly began learning Hebrew from his father (a minister) at age 5 and could read the Hebrew Bible at age 6. Jonathan Rhoades — Fellow of King's College, Cambridge.

Final Revision: Thomas Bilson (Bishop of Winchester) and Miles Smith performed the final editorial review before the text went to press. Robert Barker, the King's Printer, printed the first edition in 1611.

III. The Fifteen Translation Rules

Source: Reprinted in Gustavus S. Paine, The Men Behind the King James Bible (Baker Book House, 1959), pp. 168–170; also in Adam Nicolson, God's Secretaries (HarperCollins, 2003), pp. 226–228
Rule 1. The ordinary Bible read in the Church, commonly called the Bishops' Bible, to be followed, and as little altered as the truth of the original will permit.
Rule 2. The names of the Prophets and the Holy Writers, with the other names of the text, to be retained, as near as may be, accordingly as they were vulgarly used.
Rule 3. The old Ecclesiastical words to be kept, viz. the word church not to be translated congregation, etc.
Rule 4. When a word hath divers significations, that to be kept which hath been most commonly used by the most of the ancient Fathers, being agreeable to the propriety of the place and the analogy of faith.
Rule 5. The division of the chapters to be altered either not at all or as little as possible, if necessity so require.
Rule 6. No marginal notes at all to be affixed, but only for the explanation of the Hebrew or Greek words which cannot without some circumlocution so briefly and fitly be expressed in the text.
Rule 7. Such quotations of places to be marginally set down as shall serve for the fit reference of one Scripture to another.
Rule 8. Every particular man of each company to take the same chapter or chapters, and having translated or amended them severally by himself where he thinketh good, all to meet together, confer what they have done, and agree for their part what shall stand.
Rule 9. As any one company hath dispatched any one book in this manner they shall send it to the rest to be considered of seriously and judiciously, for his Majesty is very careful in this point.
Rule 10. If any company, upon the review of the book so sent, doubt or differ upon any place, to send them word thereof, note the place, and withal send the reasons, and withhold no good reason; till the difference be fully decided.
Rule 11. When any place of special obscurity is doubted of, letters to be directed by authority, to send to any learned man in the land for his judgment of such a place.
Rule 12. Letters to be sent from every Bishop to the rest of his clergy, admonishing them of this translation in hand; and to move and charge as many as being skillful in the tongues; and having taken pains in that kind, to send his particular observations to the company, either at Westminster, Cambridge, or Oxford.
Rule 13. The directors of each company to be the Deans of Westminster and Chester for that place and the King's professors in the Hebrew and Greek in either university.
Rule 14. These translations to be used when they agree better with the text than the Bishops' Bible: Tindoll's [Tyndale's], Matthew's, Coverdale's, Whitchurch's, Geneva.
Rule 15. Besides the said directors before mentioned, three or four of the most ancient and grave divines in that university, besides the translators, to be assigned by the vice-chancellor, upon conference with the rest of the heads, to be overseers of the translations for that place and that if any dispute arose, to be decided by the general company.
Scholar's Assessment

Adam Nicolson, in God's Secretaries: The Making of the King James Bible (HarperCollins, 2003, p. 218): "The KJV translators were the most learned men of their age in precisely the disciplines that were needed: Greek, Hebrew, Aramaic, Latin, the Church Fathers, the history of Scripture and of doctrine." Gustavus Paine, in The Men Behind the King James Bible (Baker Book House, 1959, p. 15): "In learning, in piety, in devotion to the task, the fifty-four men who began this work were without peer. No group assembled before or since has brought to a translation such combined depth in the original languages." The review process — in which every individual translator worked alone, every company then met to review each member's work, every company then sent its books to the other five companies for review, disputed passages were sent to scholars across England for outside opinion, and a final committee of twelve (two from each company) produced the unified text — was a peer-review process of extraordinary rigor by any standard, ancient or modern. John Bois's surviving notes from the final revision (discovered at Corpus Christi College, Oxford, and published by Ward Allen, Translating for King James, Vanderbilt University Press, 1969) document the care with which individual word choices were debated and documented.

⚑ The Lineage: The 1611 KJV stands at the culmination of a century of English translation, explicitly building on six prior English Bibles — themselves built from the Greek Textus Receptus and Hebrew Masoretic Text. This lineage stretches from Tyndale's 1526 Greek-based New Testament through an unbroken succession to 1611. Approximately 80% of the KJV New Testament is unchanged Tyndale.

I. The English Translation Lineage (1526–1611)

1526/1534 — William Tyndale's New Testament
The foundational English New Testament. Tyndale was the first person in history to translate the New Testament from Greek directly into English (all prior English translations — including the Wycliffe Bible of 1382 — had used Jerome's Latin Vulgate as their source text, not the original Greek). Tyndale worked from Erasmus's Greek text (the 1516 and 1522 editions) and produced translations of extraordinary literary quality and theological precision. He was strangled and burned at the stake near Brussels on October 6, 1536, for his translation work — martyred for giving England the Scripture in English. David Daniell, in William Tyndale: A Biography (Yale University Press, 1994, p. 1), estimates that "four-fifths of the Authorized Version New Testament is Tyndale." Tyndale's translation philosophy was explicit formal equivalence: "I had perceived by experience, how that it was impossible to establish the lay people in any truth except the Scripture were plainly laid before their eyes in their mother tongue" (The Obedience of a Christian Man, 1528). Tyndale also translated portions of the Old Testament (Pentateuch, Jonah, portions of Chronicles) from Hebrew before his death. His Old Testament fragments went into subsequent translations.
1535 — Miles Coverdale's Bible
The first complete printed English Bible. Coverdale worked primarily from Luther's German Bible and the Latin Vulgate, with reference to Tyndale's work, rather than directly from Hebrew and Greek. Note: although Coverdale used Luther's German as a reference source, the 1611 KJV translators worked directly from the Hebrew Masoretic Text and the Greek Textus Receptus — not from any German, Latin, or English intermediary — making the KJV independent of any theological insertions Luther introduced into his German translation, including his addition of the word allein (alone) to Romans 3:28. Despite its indirect source basis, Coverdale's prose style contributed to the literary quality of subsequent translations. His Psalter translation (used in the Book of Common Prayer) was so beautiful that it was retained even after better translations were available, influencing English liturgical language to the present day. Coverdale was later involved in producing the Great Bible (1539).
1537 — Matthew's Bible (John Rogers)
Published under the pseudonym "Thomas Matthew" by John Rogers, a close associate of Tyndale. Matthew's Bible combined Tyndale's New Testament, Tyndale's unpublished Old Testament translations (Pentateuch through 2 Chronicles), and Coverdale's work for the remaining books. It was the first English Bible to receive royal authorization — granted by Henry VIII on Cromwell's petition. John Rogers became the first Protestant martyr under Queen Mary I, burned at Smithfield on February 4, 1555 — like Tyndale, a man who died for the Scripture he helped translate. The Matthew's Bible's direct incorporation of Tyndale's unpublished Hebrew translations means that Tyndale's scholarship pervades the KJV Old Testament as well as the New.
1539 — The Great Bible (Thomas Cromwell / Henry VIII)
Commissioned by Thomas Cromwell and authorized by Henry VIII; a revised edition of Matthew's Bible, revised by Coverdale. The "Great Bible" was so named for its large physical size. Henry VIII ordered by law that a copy be placed in every English parish church — the first legally mandated universal distribution of an English Bible. Its title page depicted Henry distributing Bibles to bishops and nobles, who distribute them downward through the social hierarchy to the common people. The Great Bible served as the official church Bible until the Bishops' Bible replaced it in 1568.
1560 — The Geneva Bible (Marian Exiles)
Produced by English Protestant scholars exiled to Geneva during the reign of Queen Mary I. The Geneva Bible was the most scholarly English translation to that point, working directly from Hebrew and Greek with reference to the Latin scholars and to Calvin's commentaries. It introduced several innovations: numbered verses in the text (following Robert Estienne's 1551 Greek New Testament), running chapter summaries, marginal cross-references, and explanatory marginal notes. Its verse numbering system became universal. The Geneva Bible was the personal Bible of William Shakespeare, John Bunyan, John Donne, and the Pilgrims who sailed to America on the Mayflower in 1620. It was the dominant English Bible in private use from 1560 to well into the 17th century. The KJV translators were explicitly instructed (Rule 14) to use the Geneva Bible when it better expressed the original languages than the Bishops' Bible.
1568 — The Bishops' Bible (Archbishop Parker)
Commissioned by Archbishop Matthew Parker as an official Church of England revision of the Great Bible, intended as a scholarly alternative to the politically controversial Geneva Bible's Calvinist notes. The Bishops' Bible was translated by a committee of bishops and scholars working from the original languages. It became the official lectionary Bible of the Church of England but was never embraced by the general populace with the affection given the Geneva Bible. The KJV translators were instructed to follow it as their base text — making it the direct structural predecessor of the 1611 KJV — but were explicitly authorized to depart from it wherever the original languages required.

II. The Greek Foundation — The Textus Receptus

The New Testament of the 1611 KJV is translated from the Textus Receptus — the "Received Text" — a Greek New Testament compiled by Desiderius Erasmus in five editions between 1516 and 1535. Erasmus worked from Greek manuscripts of the Byzantine/Majority text family — the text type represented by over 5,200 of the approximately 5,800 surviving Greek New Testament manuscripts — supplemented by the Latin Vulgate for comparison and collation. The compilation of the Textus Receptus passed through several subsequent editors:

Robert Estienne (Stephanus) — Parisian printer-scholar who produced four editions of the Greek New Testament (1546, 1549, 1550, 1551). His 1550 edition is the standard "Stephanus text." His 1551 edition introduced the verse-numbering system still in use today.

Theodore Beza — Calvin's successor in Geneva; produced nine editions of the Greek New Testament (1565–1611). The KJV translators primarily used Beza's 1598 and 1611 editions.

The Elzevir Brothers — Dutch printers who published editions in 1624 and 1633; their 1633 preface first used the phrase "Textus Receptus" (received text): "Textum ergo habes, nunc ab omnibus receptum" — "you have therefore the text now received by all."

The Textus Receptus is drawn from the Antiochian/Byzantine manuscript tradition — the text in circulation in Antioch of Syria, the first-century center of the Gentile church (Acts 11:26; 13:1). Frederick Nolan, in An Inquiry into the Integrity of the Greek Vulgate (Rivington, 1815), traced the Received Text through the citations of the Church Fathers from the 2nd century forward and demonstrated that Origen, Chrysostom, Theophylact, and other patristic writers consistently cite a Greek text agreeing with the Byzantine/Received tradition rather than the Alexandrian manuscripts — establishing the Received Text's antiquity independently of manuscript counting. The approximately 5,200 manuscripts supporting the Byzantine tradition vastly outnumber the approximately 45 Alexandrian manuscripts; the Alexandrian minority includes Codex Vaticanus (B) and Codex Sinaiticus (Aleph) — the two manuscripts Westcott and Hort would elevate above all others in 1881.

III-A. Luther and the Textus Receptus — The Reformers Stood on the Same Foundation

A critical and widely overlooked fact: Martin Luther's own German New Testament translation (1522) was made from Erasmus's Textus Receptus — the same Greek manuscript tradition that underlies the 1611 KJV. Luther did not use Codex Vaticanus. He did not use Codex Sinaiticus. He worked from Erasmus's 1516 printed Greek New Testament, which drew on Byzantine/Antiochian manuscripts.

This means that when modern critical translations depart from the Textus Receptus in favor of the Alexandrian text, they are departing not only from the KJV but from Luther's own translation basis. The Westcott-Hort revision of 1881 — the foundation of every modern critical translation — represents a break from the manuscript tradition that both the KJV and Luther's Reformation-era translation were built upon.

Kenneth Strand (Adventist scholar), in German Bibles Before Luther: The Story of 14 High German Editions, further documents that Luther was not even the first to put a German Bible into print. By the time of Luther's birth in 1483, no fewer than 9 complete High German and 2 Low German printed Bibles had already been produced. By his own 1522 German New Testament publication, that number had grown to 14 High German and 4 Low German complete Bible editions — making Luther at minimum the 19th person to produce a complete German Bible, not the first. This dismantles the claim that the Catholic Church suppressed vernacular Scripture: those 18 preceding German Bible editions were produced in Catholic Germany, by Catholic printers, for Catholic readers, before Luther was born or published a single word.

Source: Kenneth Strand, German Bibles Before Luther; Joe Heschmeyer, Shameless Popery (Catholic Answers), May 30, 2024.

III. The Hebrew Foundation — The Masoretic Text

— The Masoretic Text
The Old Testament of the 1611 KJV is translated from the Masoretic Text (MT) — the authoritative Hebrew text established by the Masoretes (Jewish scribal scholars) between the 6th and 10th centuries AD, representing a text tradition traceable to manuscripts of the 2nd century BC. The Masoretes did not simply copy manuscripts; they counted every letter and word to ensure textual accuracy, developed a system of vowel points and cantillation marks to preserve correct reading traditions, and noted in the margins any word that was read differently from how it was written (Kethib/Qere apparatus). The Masoretic Text as used by the KJV translators was primarily the edition of Jacob ben Chayyim (Venice, 1525), produced from numerous manuscripts gathered from across the Jewish diaspora. The Dead Sea Scrolls, discovered in 1947, subsequently confirmed the remarkable fidelity of the Masoretic tradition: the Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a), dated to approximately 100 BC, shows the Masoretic Text to be virtually unchanged across 1,000 years of transmission.

⚑ The Principle: The 1611 KJV employs formal equivalence — every word in the original has a corresponding English word; words supplied without direct original-language counterpart are printed in italics. Post-1960s translations use dynamic equivalence — translating what the committee believes the author meant rather than what he said, invisibly embedding the translator's theology into the Scripture.

I. Translation Philosophy — The Theoretical Stakes

Formal Equivalence (Word-for-Word): The KJV's translation philosophy produces a one-to-one correspondence between source text and target text as far as English grammar allows. Where Greek or Hebrew idiom cannot be rendered word-for-word, the closest English equivalent is sought. Where a word must be supplied in English that has no counterpart in the original (because Greek lacks definite articles in certain positions, or because Hebrew tense requires additional English words to convey), the supplied word is printed in italics — a practice of radical transparency that allows any reader to see exactly what the translator added and what the original text said. No modern translation has maintained this practice consistently.

Dynamic Equivalence (Thought-for-Word): Theorized by Eugene Nida of the American Bible Society in Toward a Science of Translating (E.J. Brill, 1964, pp. 156–171; reprinted 2003), dynamic equivalence translates the thought the translator believes the author intended rather than the words the author used. Nida argued that this produced more natural English and better comprehension. The theological consequence is fundamental: wherever the Greek or Hebrew is ambiguous, contested, or theologically significant, the dynamic equivalence translator resolves the ambiguity invisibly. The reader of a dynamic equivalence translation reads the translator's theological judgment as if it were Scripture. There is no mechanism — not even italics — by which the reader can distinguish the original text from the translator's interpretation.

Miles Smith's preface to the 1611 KJV (The Translators to the Reader, 1611, as reprinted in Edgar J. Goodspeed, The Translators to the Reader, University of Chicago Press, 1935, p. 14): "we never thought from the beginning that we should need to make a new Translation, nor yet to make of a bad one a good one; but to make a good one better, or out of many good ones, one principal good one, not justly to be excepted against; that hath been our endeavour, that our mark."

II. Documented Word Changes — KJV vs. Modern Translations

Reference KJV 1611 (Word-for-Word) Modern Version Theological Consequence
Isaiah 14:12 "How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, son of the morning" NIV: "How you have fallen from heaven, morning star, son of the dawn" Removes the proper name identifying Satan in his pre-fall state; "morning star" is a title applied to Christ in Revelation 22:16, creating confusion of identity
1 Timothy 3:16 "God was manifest in the flesh" NIV: "He appeared in a body"; NASB: "He who was revealed in the flesh" Removes the explicit declaration of Christ's deity. Follows Codex Vaticanus (B) which has "OS" (who/he) rather than "ΘΕΟΣ" (God) — a variant rejected by 99%+ of manuscripts
Colossians 1:14 "redemption through his blood, even the forgiveness of sins" NIV/NASB: "redemption, the forgiveness of sins" — "through his blood" omitted entirely Removes the blood atonement from the explicit statement of redemption. The phrase is present in the Received Text but absent from Alexandrian manuscripts
Matthew 18:11 "For the Son of man is come to save that which was lost" NIV/NASB/ESV: Entire verse omitted (moved to footnote "some manuscripts include") A complete statement of Christ's redemptive mission disappears from the text. Present in Received Text / Byzantine tradition; absent in Alexandrian manuscripts Westcott-Hort privileged
Acts 8:37 "I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God" (entire verse — Philip's requirement for baptism) NIV/NASB/ESV: Entire verse omitted The doctrinal confession required before baptism disappears from Acts. The Ethiopian eunuch is baptized without the recorded profession of faith. Present in Received Text; absent in Alexandrian manuscripts
Daniel 3:25 "the form of the fourth is like the Son of God" NIV: "the fourth looks like a son of the gods"; NASB same Transforms a Messianic identification (Nebuchadnezzar recognizing the Son of God) into a pagan polytheistic statement. "Gods" (elohim) can mean the divine Son in Hebrew theology
Mark 7:19 "purging all meats" (referring to the digestive process) NIV: "(In saying this, Jesus declared all foods clean)" — parenthetical translator interpretation inserted as scripture The words "Jesus declared all foods clean" appear in NO Greek manuscript. The NIV translator's theological conclusion is inserted into the text in parentheses — dynamic equivalence making interpretation indistinguishable from Scripture
John 1:18 "the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father" NASB/ESV: "the only begotten God"; NIV: "the one and only Son" The NASB/ESV reading follows Vaticanus; "only begotten God" is an awkward reading that collapses the distinction between the Father and Son in the immediate context of "who is in the bosom of the Father"
Luke 24:51 "he was parted from them, and carried up into heaven" RSV/NRSV: "carried up into heaven" omitted in some editions as a "later addition" Luke's account of the Ascension is placed in doubt. The phrase is present in the Received Text and in the vast majority of manuscripts
Isaiah 7:14 "Behold, a virgin shall conceive" RSV/NRSV: "Behold, a young woman shall conceive" The Hebrew almah is rendered "young woman" rather than "virgin" — removing the specific prophetic force of the virgin birth announcement as Matthew 1:23 applies it. The LXX uses parthenos (virgin) for this verse.
Luther's Own Insertion — "Allein" (Alone) — Romans 3:28

The clearest documented case of a translator inserting his theology into the text — rather than translating the text — is Luther's own German Bible. In Romans 3:28, Luther inserted the word allein (alone) where no Greek manuscript contains it. The verse in Greek reads "a man is justified by faith apart from works of the law." Luther rendered it: "So halten wir nun dafür, daß der Mensch gerecht werde ohne des Gesetzes Werke, allein durch den Glauben" — "we hold that a man is justified without works of the law, by faith alone."

When challenged on this insertion, Luther replied: "If your Papist annoys you with the word (allein), tell him straightaway: Dr. Martin Luther will have it so... I will have it so, and I order it to be so, and my will is reason enough. I know very well that the word allein is not in the Latin or the Greek text and it was not necessary for the Papists to teach me that." (Luther's Open Letter on Translating, 1530)

This is the foundational act of dynamic equivalence: the translator's theological conclusion inserted as Scripture. The 1611 KJV — translated under 15 formal rules requiring committee accountability and transparency about supplied words — does not add alone to Romans 3:28. The KJV reads: "Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law." The word "alone" is not in the text; the KJV does not put it there.

Dean Burgon's Summary Assessment

Dean John William Burgon, The Revision Revised (John Murray, 1883, p. 230): "The Revisionists have altered the Greek Text in no less than 5,337 places. They have similarly altered the English in not fewer than 36,000 places — the most part of the alterations being for the worse." Burgon spent his scholarly career collating manuscripts in the libraries of Rome, Paris, Oxford, Cambridge, the British Museum, the monastery of St. Catherine (Sinai), and the libraries of Mt. Athos — the most extensive first-hand manuscript examination undertaken by any 19th-century scholar. His conclusion after direct examination: the Received Text, as embodied in the King James Bible, is not inferior to but superior to the Critical Text of Westcott and Hort.

⚑ The Historical Record: King James I authorized the 1611 Bible at the proposal of others, organized the scholarly enterprise, stayed almost entirely out of the translation decisions, survived an assassination attempt while the translation was underway, and was subsequently slandered into infamy by a dismissed court official whose posthumous character assassination has passed into popular history almost entirely unchallenged.

I. Who Was King James I?

James VI of Scotland (1566–1625) became James I of England upon the death of Queen Elizabeth I in March 1603. He had been King of Scotland since 1567 — ascending to the throne as an infant after his mother Mary Queen of Scots was forced to abdicate. He was raised under the tutorship of the Scottish reformer George Buchanan, one of the leading classical scholars of the 16th century, and received an education of extraordinary depth: Latin, Greek, French, and theology were all learned in childhood. James wrote extensively and seriously throughout his life: The Trew Law of Free Monarchies (1598), Basilikon Doron (1599, a treatise on kingship addressed to his son), Daemonologie (1597, a theological study of witchcraft), a commentary on Revelation, a paraphrase of the Psalms, and numerous other works. Jenny Wormald, in the most cited modern scholarly article on James — "James VI and I: Two Kings or One?" (History, 68, 1983, p. 189) — argues that "the hostile English sources have so thoroughly dominated the historiography that the substantial achievements of his 36-year Scottish reign have been systematically ignored." Alan Stewart, in The Cradle King: The Life of James VI & I (Chatto & Windus, 2003, p. xii), states: "James was a man of genuine theological seriousness, serious enough to convene a conference of bishops and scholars within months of arriving in England specifically to address ecclesiastical concerns and propose a new Bible translation. That the resulting Bible bore his name and was attributed to his political influence rather than to the 47 scholars who produced it is one of the great ironies of English cultural history."

II. James's Role in the Translation — Minimal, Structural, and Appropriate

James's documented contributions to the translation were: (1) enthusiastic endorsement of Reynolds's proposal at Hampton Court; (2) organization of the six-company structure; (3) appointment of company directors; (4) stipulation of the fifteen rules; (5) one substantive word suggestion — that "Church" should be used rather than "Congregation" (the Puritan preference), which was one of the issues in Rule 3. That is the complete documented list. James did not attend any company meetings. He did not review any books in progress. He was not consulted on any translation disputes. The finished text was not submitted to him for approval before printing. The title "Authorized Version" refers to the fact that James authorized the project — not that he authorized specific translation decisions. The words of the 1611 KJV are the words of 47 scholars, not the words of a king. Gustavus Paine, The Men Behind the King James Bible (Baker Book House, 1959, p. 56): "James gave the translators their commission and their rules and then left them entirely alone to do their work. The notion that he influenced the translation is without historical foundation."

III. The Gunpowder Plot — November 5, 1605

In the first year of the KJV translation — while the six companies were completing their initial drafts — a conspiracy was formed to kill King James, the royal family, and the entire Parliament of England in a single act of coordinated mass assassination. The conspirators were English Catholics led by Robert Catesby, a Warwickshire gentleman of strong Catholic conviction. The motivation: King James's continuation of Elizabethan penal laws against Catholics, despite initial signals of tolerance at his accession. The plan: 36 barrels of gunpowder were transported into a rented cellar beneath the House of Lords and concealed under a layer of coal and firewood. The State Opening of Parliament, scheduled for November 5, 1605, would bring King James, Queen Anne, Prince Henry, and the entire aristocracy of England into the building simultaneously. Guy Fawkes, a soldier with extensive military experience in the Spanish Netherlands, was designated to light the fuse and escape before detonation. The conspirators: Robert Catesby (leader), Thomas Percy, John Wright, Christopher Wright, Thomas Wintour, Robert Wintour, Thomas Bates, Robert Keyes, Ambrose Rookwood, Sir Everard Digby, Francis Tresham, John Grant, and Guy Fawkes. The discovery: On October 26, 1605, Lord Monteagle received an anonymous letter warning him not to attend Parliament on November 5. Monteagle reported the letter to Robert Cecil, Earl of Salisbury, and the government. On the night of November 4–5, a search of the Parliament building discovered Guy Fawkes in the cellar with the gunpowder. Under torture, Fawkes revealed the other conspirators. Catesby and several others died in a firefight at Holbeche House, Staffordshire, on November 8; the surviving conspirators were tried and executed by hanging, drawing, and quartering in January 1606. The Gunpowder Plot State Papers are preserved in the National Archives (PRO, SP 14/216, various documents). King James personally examined the conspirators and wrote A Discourse of the Manner of the Discovery of this Late Intended Treason (1605). Parliament enacted the Observance of 5th November Act 1605, declaring November 5 a national day of thanksgiving for the king's deliverance. The act was not repealed until 1859. The historical significance: the king who commissioned the English Bible was targeted for assassination in the middle of the translation process, survived, and saw the translation completed six years later.

IV. Sir Anthony Weldon — The Slander Campaign and Its Sources

The negative popular image of James I — as physically ungainly, personally cowardly, politically incompetent, and morally degenerate — derives almost entirely from a single biased source: Sir Anthony Weldon's The Court and Character of King James, published in 1650, twenty-three years after James's death in 1625. Weldon's Conflict of Interest: Sir Anthony Weldon served as Clerk of the Kitchen at James's court. In 1617, he accompanied James on a royal progress to Scotland and, during the journey, composed private written notes describing Scots and Scottish culture in viciously contemptuous terms. James discovered these notes. Weldon was permanently dismissed from court and stripped of his position. He spent the rest of his life — and his son spent additional years after Weldon's death circa 1649 — composing what historians have recognized as a document of personal revenge dressed in the language of historical memoir. The Posthumous Publication Strategy: By waiting until after James's death, Weldon ensured that his subject could not defend himself, challenge the characterizations, or hold him accountable for specific claims. By publishing twenty-three years after James's death — when most eyewitnesses were themselves dead — Weldon minimized the possibility of public contradiction from those who had known James personally. What Historians Say: D. Harris Wilson, King James VI and I (Jonathan Cape, 1956, p. 3): "Weldon's account is a libel dressed as history. His descriptions of James's personal habits, his appearance, his speech, and his alleged cowardice are the productions of a man who hated his former master and saw posthumous publication as a safe vehicle for his hatred." Alan Stewart, The Cradle King (Chatto & Windus, 2003, p. xii): "Weldon's Court and Character has been remarkably influential, and remarkably uncritically accepted. Its specific claims — that James was slobbering, tongue-too-large, cowardly, and controlled by favorites — reappear in popular history to the present day, almost always without the attribution to their biased source." Jenny Wormald, "James VI and I: Two Kings or One?" (History, 68, 1983, p. 201): "The problem with the English sources is that the hostile ones — Weldon, Osborne, Harrington — have been used as primary evidence when they are demonstrably partisan, while the favorable sources — Goodman, Cornwallis — have been neglected." Francis Osborne — whose Traditional Memoirs on the Reign of King James the First (1658) is the other major hostile account — was similarly a political opponent with personal grievances who published after James's death. Peter Heylyn's Refutation (1659): The contemporary printed refutation of Weldon is Peter Heylyn's Examen Historicum (London, 1659; Wing H1699; available EEBO) — written while eyewitnesses of the Jacobean court were still alive. Heylyn dismissed Weldon's book as "an infamous libel" and documented specific factual misrepresentations within it. Goodman independently described Weldon as the most "malicious-minded author" he had ever read, adding that Weldon had "such poor and mean observations" — a verdict from a court insider who knew the same facts Weldon claimed to report. Both assessments are cited in D. Harris Wilson, King James VI and I (Jonathan Cape, 1956, p. 3). The Contrasting Account: Bishop Godfrey Goodman, who served at James's court and left a manuscript memoir (published in 1839 as The Court of King James the First, Bentley, London), presents a strikingly different picture: a man of genuine learning, deep theological seriousness, and real political competence whose reputation was systematically destroyed by enemies who outlived him and controlled the printing presses after his death.

⚑ The Campaign: The coordinated scholarly effort to displace the 1611 KJV began formally in 1881 with Westcott and Hort's new Greek text and the Revised Version — and has continued to the present. The campaign has operated on three fronts: (1) producing a new Greek "Critical Text" from Alexandrian manuscripts; (2) translating multiple competing English Bibles from that text; (3) arguing that the KJV is archaic, inaccurate, and based on inferior manuscripts. All three claims have been refuted by scholars of the first rank.

I. Westcott & Hort (1881) — The Opening of the Campaign

Brooke Foss Westcott (Regius Professor of Divinity, Cambridge; later Bishop of Durham) and Fenton John Anthony Hort (Hulsean Professor of Divinity, Cambridge) worked privately for twenty-eight years (1853–1881) on a new Greek New Testament text before its simultaneous publication with the Revised Version in 1881. Their text departed from the Received Text in approximately 5,604 places. Their methodology privileged two Alexandrian manuscripts — Codex Vaticanus (B, Vatican Library, dated to the 4th century) and Codex Sinaiticus (Aleph, St. Catherine's Monastery, Sinai, dated to the 4th century) — over the approximately 5,200 Byzantine/Majority manuscripts that support the Received Text. Westcott and Hort called Vaticanus and Sinaiticus the "Neutral Text" — an unscientific designation rejected by subsequent textual critics. Their argument: these two manuscripts are older (4th century vs. the Byzantine manuscripts, most of which date to the 9th–14th centuries) and therefore closer to the originals. The response: (1) The age of a manuscript does not determine its accuracy; a late copy of an early accurate archetype is more reliable than an early copy of a corrupted one. (2) The patristic citations of the 2nd–3rd centuries — which predate both Vaticanus and Sinaiticus — agree with the Byzantine/Majority text rather than the Alexandrian, meaning the Byzantine text type is historically earlier even if the surviving manuscripts are later copies (Frederick Nolan, An Inquiry into the Integrity of the Greek Vulgate, 1815; Jakob Van Bruggen, The Ancient Text of the New Testament, 1976). (3) Vaticanus and Sinaiticus disagree with each other in 3,036 places in the Gospels alone — demonstrating that at least one of the two manuscripts Westcott and Hort called "Neutral" is substantially corrupted (Herman C. Hoskier, Codex B and Its Allies, 2 vols., Bernard Quaritch, 1914, Vol. 2, pp. 1–420).

II. Dean John William Burgon — The Scholar Who Demolished the Westcott-Hort Theory

Dean John William Burgon (1813–1888) — Dean of Chichester Cathedral from 1876 — was the most rigorous New Testament textual scholar of the 19th century and the foremost contemporary critic of the Westcott-Hort theory. He had personally collated manuscripts in the libraries of Rome (Vatican Library), Paris (Bibliothèque Nationale), Oxford (Bodleian Library), Cambridge (University Library), the British Museum, Mount Sinai (St. Catherine's Monastery), and the libraries and monasteries of Mount Athos — at the time, the most extensive first-hand manuscript collation undertaken by any living scholar. His published responses to the Westcott-Hort text include: The Last Twelve Verses of the Gospel According to S. Mark (James Parker, 1871) — a defense of Mark 16:9–20 against early Critical Text omissions; The Revision Revised (John Murray, 1883, 640 pages) — a comprehensive demolition of the Westcott-Hort methodology; The Traditional Text of the Holy Gospels (George Bell, 1896, posthumous); The Causes of the Corruption of the Traditional Text of the Holy Gospels (George Bell, 1896, posthumous). Key findings from The Revision Revised (1883): "The impurity of the Texts exhibited by Codices B and Aleph is not a matter of opinion but of fact... In the Gospels alone [Aleph] differs from the Received Text in 8972 places" (p. 12). "I am able to demonstrate that the Text of [Westcott and Hort] is hopelessly astray, being based on a fatally false theory, viz. that the two oldest Codices — Vaticanus (B) and Sinaiticus (Aleph) — do, in the main, represent the genuine Text of the New Testament" (p. 16). "The result of our investigation is this: the commonly received Text, the Textus Receptus, is found to be incomparably nearer the Truth than the rival productions of Lachmann, Tischendorf, Tregelles, Westcott and Hort" (p. 340). The institutional response to Burgon's demolition was not scholarly rebuttal but professional marginalization: the Critical Text was promoted despite his objections, and Burgon's works were allowed to go out of print. They were reprinted in the 20th century by the Dean Burgon Society and remain in print today.

III. The Statistical Case — Manuscript Evidence for the Received Text

Wilbur Pickering (Th.M., Dallas Theological Seminary; Ph.D., University of Toronto, linguistics), The Identity of the New Testament Text (Thomas Nelson, 1977; 4th ed., 2014): "The evidence is overwhelming that the original text of the New Testament has been preserved in the Majority Text tradition. The Majority Text has better manuscript support, better patristic support, better lectionary support, and better internal evidence than the Critical Text" (pp. 166–168). Herman C. Hoskier, Codex B and Its Allies: A Study and an Indictment (Bernard Quaritch, 1914, 2 vols.): systematic comparison demonstrating that Codex Vaticanus and Codex Sinaiticus — the two manuscripts on which the entire Critical Text enterprise rests — disagree with each other in 3,036 places in the Gospels alone. If these two manuscripts constitute the "Neutral Text" (Westcott-Hort's designation), they are a "Neutral Text" internally contradicting itself in every 100 verses. Frederick Nolan, An Inquiry into the Integrity of the Greek Vulgate or Received Text of the New Testament (Rivington, 1815): the earliest modern scholarly defense of the Received Text, tracing its textual tradition through patristic citations from the 2nd century forward, demonstrating that the Church Fathers of Alexandria itself — Origen and Clement — do not consistently cite the Alexandrian text type now named for them. Edward F. Hills (Th.D., Harvard Divinity School; Ph.D., Columbia University), The King James Version Defended (Christian Research Press, 1956; 4th ed., 1984): the most comprehensive theological-textual defense of the KJV, arguing from the Reformed doctrine of providential preservation that the Textus Receptus represents the text the Holy Spirit guided the Church to preserve and use: "Just as God guided the early Church to collect the true New Testament canon, so also God guided the Reformers to use the True New Testament text" (p. 108). Jakob Van Bruggen, The Ancient Text of the New Testament (Premier, 1976): demonstrating that the Church Fathers of the 2nd and 3rd centuries — writing before either Vaticanus or Sinaiticus were produced — cite a Greek text agreeing with the Byzantine/Majority tradition, proving the Byzantine text type is historically earlier than the Alexandrian even if surviving Byzantine manuscripts are dated later.

IV. The Modern Discrediting Campaign — Three False Claims

Claim #1: "The KJV is written in archaic language that modern readers cannot understand."
Refutation: The KJV's Jacobean English (the English of Shakespeare, Bunyan, and Milton) is comprehensible to any reader who engages with it for thirty minutes. The "archaic language" argument proves too much: it would require producing a new translation every generation, producing an infinite and irresolvable series of competing Scripture texts. Moreover, the argument misunderstands language acquisition: readers regularly learn the specialized vocabulary of science, law, medicine, and literature without insisting that those fields rewrite themselves in the latest colloquial register. If anything, the KJV's slightly elevated register — its "thee," "thou," and "hath" — preserves the second-person singular/plural distinction that Greek and Hebrew maintain but that modern English has collapsed in "you," a collapse that loses meaning in numerous passages.

Claim #2: "The KJV is based on inferior or late manuscripts."
Refutation: See the evidence of Burgon, Hoskier, Nolan, Van Bruggen, and Pickering above. The "inferior manuscripts" claim reverses the actual manuscript evidence. The Received Text is supported by over 5,200 of approximately 5,800 surviving Greek manuscripts, by the lectionary tradition, by the patristic citations of the 2nd–3rd centuries, and by the continuous tradition of the Church from the Reformation backward. The Alexandrian manuscripts (Vaticanus, Sinaiticus) upon which the Critical Text is based are supported by approximately 45 manuscripts, agree with each other only imperfectly (3,036 disagreements in the Gospels alone), and were not followed by the Church Fathers who had access to them.

Claim #3: "The KJV was produced by a politically motivated king."
Refutation: King James's documented role in the translation is limited to (1) approving the project, (2) organizing the companies, (3) establishing the fifteen rules, and (4) one word suggestion. The translation was produced by 47 scholars of extraordinary combined learning working under a rigorous peer-review process over seven years. James was nearly assassinated in the middle of the project. The claim that the Bible bears his political imprint rests on the posthumous character assassination of Sir Anthony Weldon — a dismissed court official whose revenge memoir was published twenty-three years after James's death and accepted by subsequent popular historians without critical evaluation of its source bias.

V. The Protestant Mythology Machine — How the Anti-KJV Campaign Was Built

The coordinated campaign against the KJV did not arise in a vacuum. It was built on a parallel campaign of historical revision that manufactured a heroic Protestant founding narrative — the same narrative that, after 1840, became the intellectual atmosphere in which Westcott and Hort's Greek critical text (1881) was produced and accepted.

Historian Samuel L. Young, writing in Lutheran Quarterly ("How Luther Became the Mythical 'Here I Stand' Hero"), documents that the famous "Here I Stand" speech attributed to Luther at the Diet of Worms (1521) does not appear in any eyewitness account of the event. It first entered the British and American press as the dominant version of events after 1840 — the same decade that British scholars began preparing what would become the Revised Version (1881). Young writes: "Luther could simultaneously be touted as the champion of democracy, evangelical religion, human rights, individualism, free thought, progress, and modernity" — whatever the agenda required.

The manufactured Luther served three overlapping agendas simultaneously: (1) Protestant apologists who needed a founding hero to justify separation from Rome and its textual tradition; (2) secularists and nationalists who needed an "individual against institutional authority" archetype; and (3) British academic revisionists who needed a historical narrative in which received ecclesiastical texts were inherently suspect and "original manuscripts" were inherently superior. All three agendas converged in the Westcott-Hort project.

Kenneth Strand (Adventist scholar), in German Bibles Before Luther, documents that by Luther's own publication there were already 14 High German and 4 Low German complete printed Bibles — yet the narrative that Luther "gave people the Bible for the first time" became standard. This same pattern of false historical claim — presented as fact, repeated by educators, never verified against primary sources — is the operational template of the modern KJV discrediting campaign. The claim that the KJV rests on "inferior late manuscripts" is structurally identical: stated confidently, repeated by educators, based on assumptions that collapse under primary-source scrutiny.

⚑ The Complete Record: From the Septuagint in 285 BC to the present day — a 2,300-year record of Scripture translation that shows the 1611 KJV standing at the apex of a rigorous formal-equivalence tradition, followed by a post-1950 proliferation of dynamic-equivalence versions that fractured unified textual authority for the first time in Protestant history.

Ancient & Patristic Era
c. 285–132 BC Septuagint (LXX) — Greek Old Testament
Translation of the Hebrew Scriptures into Greek, produced in Alexandria, Egypt, by Jewish scholars — tradition holds 72 elders over 72 days for the Pentateuch (Letter of Aristeas, c. 200 BC). Extended to the full Hebrew canon over subsequent decades. The LXX became the Scripture of the Greek-speaking Jewish diaspora and the primary Old Testament source cited by the New Testament authors and the Church Fathers. When Matthew 1:23 cites Isaiah 7:14 with parthenos (virgin), he follows the LXX — a fact critical for evaluating later translations that use "young woman." The LXX is the source text for the Coptic, Ethiopic, Armenian, and Georgian Old Testaments.
c. AD 50–95 Greek New Testament — Original Autographs
27 books composed in Koine Greek by Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, Paul, Peter, James, and Jude. Circulated and copied across Mediterranean congregations. No original autograph survives. The Byzantine/Majority tradition (5,200+ manuscripts) preserves the dominant transmission form. The Alexandrian tradition (45 manuscripts) preserves a variant form found primarily in Egypt.
AD 382–405 Latin Vulgate — Jerome
Commissioned by Pope Damasus I. Jerome translated the OT directly from Hebrew and the NT from Greek into Latin — authoritative Scripture of the Western Church for 1,100+ years. Declared official Catholic Bible at the Council of Trent (1546). Jerome's Latin shaped Western theological vocabulary in decisive ways — his poenitentiam agite (do penance) for Greek metanoeite (repent) embedded a penitential system into the Latin text. The Vulgate's dominance explains why the Wycliffe Bible (1382) was translated from Latin rather than Greek and Hebrew.
c. AD 500 Peshitta — Syriac Bible
Standard Syriac translation of the Bible used by Middle Eastern Syriac-speaking churches. Its NT excludes 2 Peter, 2–3 John, Jude, and Revelation — books accepted later in the Western canon. Represents an independent textual tradition; agrees with the Byzantine/Majority text in the great majority of contested passages.
Early English Era (1380–1568)
1382 / 1395 Wycliffe Bible — John Wycliffe & Nicholas of Hereford
First complete English Bible — translated from Jerome's Latin Vulgate, not from Hebrew or Greek. Never printed (250 handwritten manuscripts survive). Wycliffe was condemned as a heretic; his bones were exhumed and burned in 1428. His associate John Purvey revised the translation c. 1395. The Lollard movement spread the text in secret under official suppression. It carries the mistranslations embedded in the Vulgate rather than the original languages.
1516 Erasmus Greek New Testament — Textus Receptus Foundation
First printed Greek NT (Novum Instrumentum omne, Basel, 1516). Revised in five editions (1516–1535). The foundation of the Textus Receptus: Erasmus → Stephanus (1550) → Beza (1598) → Elzevir (1633, first use of "Textus Receptus"). Without Erasmus there is no Tyndale; without Tyndale, no KJV. The printing press (Gutenberg, c. 1450) made mass distribution of this text — and all subsequent Scripture — possible for the first time in history.
1522 / 1534 Luther's German New Testament & Bible — Built on the Textus Receptus
Martin Luther translated the NT (1522) from Erasmus's Textus Receptus (1516 edition) — the same Greek manuscript tradition underlying the KJV. His complete German Bible appeared in 1534. Critically: Luther was NOT the first to produce a German Bible. Kenneth Strand (Adventist scholar), German Bibles Before Luther: The Story of 14 High German Editions, documents that by Luther's birth in 1483, 9 complete High German and 2 Low German printed Bibles already existed. By his publication, 14 High German and 4 Low German editions had preceded him — produced by Catholic printers for Catholic readers, disproving the narrative that the Church withheld Scripture. Luther also inserted the word allein (alone) into Romans 3:28 where no Greek manuscript contains it, then explicitly defended the insertion as his own authority rather than the text's (Luther, Open Letter on Translating, 1530).
1526 / 1534 Tyndale New Testament — First Greek-to-English Translation
William Tyndale — first English NT translated directly from Greek. Also translated Pentateuch and Jonah from Hebrew. Goal: "a boy that driveth the plough shall know more of the Scripture than thou dost." Strangled and burned at the stake near Brussels, October 6, 1536. Approximately 80% of the KJV New Testament is unchanged Tyndale (David Daniell, William Tyndale: A Biography, Yale, 1994, p. 1).
1535 Coverdale Bible — First Complete Printed English Bible
Miles Coverdale. Translated primarily from Luther's German and Latin Vulgate (not directly from Hebrew and Greek). His Psalter — retained in the Book of Common Prayer — is so beautiful it persisted in liturgical use long after more accurate translations existed.
1537 Matthew's Bible — First Royally Authorized English Bible
John Rogers (pseudonym "Thomas Matthew"). Combined Tyndale's NT, Tyndale's unpublished OT translations, and Coverdale's remaining books. First English Bible with royal authorization (Henry VIII). Rogers was the first Protestant martyr under Queen Mary I, burned at Smithfield, February 4, 1555.
1539 Great Bible — First Mandated for Every English Parish Church
Commissioned by Thomas Cromwell; revised by Coverdale. Named for its large folio size. Henry VIII ordered by law that a copy be chained in every English parish church — first universal mandated Scripture distribution in English history. Official lectionary Bible until the Bishops' Bible (1568).
1560 Geneva Bible — The Scholars' Bible; Shakespeare's & the Pilgrims' Bible
Produced by English Protestant exiles in Geneva during Queen Mary's reign. First English Bible with numbered verses throughout. Used by Shakespeare, Bunyan, Donne, and the Mayflower Pilgrims (1620). Most popular private Bible from 1560 to mid-17th century. King James objected to its Calvinist marginal notes (justifying disobedience to kings), not its translation quality. The KJV translators were instructed (Rule 14) to use it when it better expressed the original languages.
1568 Bishops' Bible — Official Church of England Revision; KJV Base Text
Commissioned by Archbishop Matthew Parker. Official Church of England Bible — never embraced by the public as fully as the Geneva Bible. Designated as the base text for the 1611 KJV translators (Rule 1), who were authorized and frequently chose to depart from it wherever the original languages required.
The KJV Era (1604–1769)
⚑ 1611 King James Bible — The Authorized Version
Produced 1604–1611 by 47 scholars in six companies at Westminster, Oxford, and Cambridge. Formal equivalence from the Textus Receptus (NT) and Masoretic Text (OT), building on six prior English translations under fifteen governing rules. Printed by Robert Barker, 1611. Dominant English Bible for 341 years. Used by an estimated 1 billion people over four centuries. Its prose shaped English more profoundly than any other single document: "still small voice," "salt of the earth," "thorn in the flesh," "the spirit is willing but the flesh is weak," "an eye for an eye" — hundreds of phrases entered English from the KJV. No English translation before or since was produced by a body of scholars of comparable linguistic depth under a comparably rigorous peer-review process.
1769 Oxford Standard Text — The KJV Text in Current Use
Benjamin Blayney (Hertford College, Oxford) standardized spelling, punctuation, and italics across 158 years of reprinted KJV editions. The text printed in virtually all modern KJV Bibles is the 1769 Oxford Standard Text — orthographically modernized but not re-translated. The translation itself remains that of the original 47 scholars.
19th-Century Revision Era (1881–1901)
1881 Westcott-Hort Greek Text & English Revised Version (RV)
After 28 years of private work (1853–1881), B.F. Westcott and F.J.A. Hort published a new Greek NT privileging Codex Vaticanus and Sinaiticus over 5,200 Byzantine manuscripts. Simultaneously published with the Church of England's Revised Version — departing from the KJV in over 36,000 places (Burgon, The Revision Revised, 1883). The Westcott-Hort text became the foundation of the modern Nestle-Aland Critical Text. Immediately challenged by Dean Burgon; never universally accepted but institutionally adopted in academic NT scholarship.
1901 American Standard Version (ASV)
American revision of the 1881 RV. Renders "Jehovah" throughout the OT rather than "LORD." Used the Westcott-Hort Critical Text for the NT. Considered highly literal for its era. Base text for the NASB (1971) and RSV (1952).
The Proliferation Era (1952–Present) — Post-Day Agenda
1952 Revised Standard Version (RSV) — National Council of Churches
First major post-war English Bible; funded by the National Council of Churches. Rendered Isaiah 7:14 as "young woman" rather than "virgin" — immediately controversial; one minister burned a copy with a blowtorch and mailed the ashes to the translation committee. Based on the Nestle-Aland Critical Text for the NT. First major crack in the KJV's 341-year dominance as the singular English Protestant Scripture.
1965 Amplified Bible
Published by Zondervan/Lockman Foundation. Inserts multiple translation options and brackets directly into the biblical text — embedding interpretive decisions as if they were Scripture. Represents the logical extreme of dynamic equivalence: the translator's commentary is structurally indistinguishable from the original words.
1971 New American Standard Bible (NASB)
Lockman Foundation revision of the ASV using the Nestle-Aland Critical Text for NT. Widely adopted in evangelical seminaries as a "more literal" alternative to the NIV. Omits or brackets verses present in the Byzantine tradition (Matthew 18:11, Acts 8:37, and others). Updated in 1977, 1995, and 2020.
1973 / 1978 New International Version (NIV)
Most commercially successful modern Bible translation (International Bible Society / Zondervan). Dynamic equivalence. Departs from the KJV in over 64,000 places (Riplinger, New Age Bible Versions, 1993, p. 56). Omits entire Byzantine-tradition verses. Mark 7:19 inserts "(In saying this, Jesus declared all foods clean)" — words found in no Greek manuscript. Updated 1984 and 2011 (2011 edition introduced gender-neutral language throughout).
1982 New King James Version (NKJV)
Thomas Nelson. Uses the Received Text for the NT but includes extensive footnotes promoting Critical Text (Westcott-Hort) readings — embedding doubt about the text it purports to translate in its own margins. The NU footnotes (Nestle-Aland/United Bible Societies) indicate Critical Text variants throughout.
1989 New Revised Standard Version (NRSV)
National Council of Churches revision of the RSV. First major English Bible to introduce systematic gender-neutral language — rendering Hebrew and Greek masculine generic nouns and pronouns with gender-neutral equivalents. This is a policy commitment to contemporary gender ideology imposed onto the text, not a translation of any manuscript. Updated as the NRSVue (2021).
1996 / 2004 New Living Translation (NLT)
Tyndale House Publishers. Complete rewrite of the Living Bible paraphrase (Kenneth Taylor, 1971). Fully dynamic equivalence — thought-for-thought. Functions as commentary in many passages. The original Living Bible was openly acknowledged by its author as a paraphrase of his own opinions; the NLT is marketed as a "translation." By 2010, the second-best-selling English Bible after the NIV.
2001 English Standard Version (ESV) — Crossway
Conservative evangelical alternative to the gender-neutral NRSV. Based on the Nestle-Aland 27th edition Critical Text. Claims "essentially literal" translation philosophy but follows Critical Text omissions (brackets/footnotes for Matthew 18:11, Acts 8:37, Mark 16:9–20, John 7:53–8:11, and others). Rapidly adopted by Reformed and Presbyterian seminaries.
2004 / 2017 Holman Christian Standard Bible / Christian Standard Bible (HCSB / CSB)
Holman Bible Publishers (Southern Baptist Convention publishing arm). Claims "optimal equivalence." The 2017 CSB introduced limited gender-neutral language. Notable for rendering "Yahweh" in selected OT passages inconsistently alongside "LORD."
2011 / 2021+ NIV (2011), NRSVue (2021), and the Ongoing Revision Cycle
The 2011 NIV revision introduced comprehensive gender-neutral language, triggering backlash from the Southern Baptist Convention and others who had endorsed the 1984 NIV. The 2021 NRSVue extended gender-neutral language further. The ongoing revision cycle — in which major translations are updated every 10–30 years — produces precisely what Dr. Richard Day described in 1969: no single authoritative English text, a marketplace of competing versions, and the concept of "what the Bible says" contested at the translation level before any interpretation begins.
What the Timeline Demonstrates
From 285 BC to 1611 — 1,896 years — Scripture translation moved toward greater fidelity to the original languages, culminating in the formal-equivalence achievement of the KJV. From 1611 to 1952 — 341 years — the KJV stood essentially alone as English Protestant Scripture. From 1952 to the present — 73 years — at least 15 major competing English translations have been produced, all based on the Westcott-Hort Critical Text, all using dynamic equivalence to varying degrees, all omitting or bracketing Byzantine-tradition passages, and all contributing to the fragmentation Dr. Day described as planned. The KJV is not one option among many — it is the product of 1,896 years of textual development, 47 scholars of exceptional learning, and a seven-year rigorous peer-review process, now surrounded by competitors produced in less time by smaller committees with less combined linguistic depth and explicit commercial motivation.

📌 The Pattern

These removals are not random. Across all categories they cluster around five doctrinal areas: (1) the deity of Christ — verses establishing Jesus as God manifest in flesh; (2) the blood atonement — references to Christ's blood as the basis of redemption; (3) spiritual discipline — prayer, fasting, and the reality of demonic activity; (4) the reality of hell — verses affirming eternal consequence; and (5) the specific Name — passages identifying God by His covenant Name, JEHOVAH or LORD.

The authority behind these changes is the 1881 Westcott & Hort Greek critical text, which departed from 5,200+ Byzantine manuscripts in favour of two Alexandrian manuscripts — Codex Vaticanus (kept in the Vatican Library, never accessible to Protestant translators until the 19th century) and Codex Sinaiticus (discovered at St. Catherine's Monastery in 1844 by Tischendorf, who initially took it without permission). Every modern critical translation — NIV (1973/1984/2011), NASB (1971/1995/2020), ESV (2001/2016), RSV (1952), NLT (1996/2004), CSB (2017) — rests on this Alexandrian foundation.
